SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, there is no difficulty in  sharing the 
numbers with the House. This case goes back to Dece mber, 2002 when the 
recruitment rules for the post of inspector were am ended, and the cadre 
restructuring took place with effect from 7.12.2002 . As a result of the 
restructuring, the number of sanctioned posts of in spector declined from 645 
to 511. However, in a case filed in the Andhra Prad esh High Court, the High 
Court directed that the vacancies must be calculate d on the basis that was 
prevailing prior to the cadre restructuring on 7th December, 2002 and as per 
the old RRs of 1979. The Government accepted the An dhra Pradesh High 
Court judgement, constituted a reviewed DPC, and th e review DPC promoted 
all eligible SC and ST officers from the feeder cat egory to the category of 
inspector. The numbers are following: 
Total number of officers promoted: 171 
General category       : 128 
SC : 27 
ST 16 
in terms of percentages, the SC candidates, who hav e been promoted, 
constitute 15.8 per cent and the ST candidates cons titute 9.4 per cent. 
According to the information available with me, all  the SC and the ST 
candidates eligible for promotion in the feeder cat egory under the H.C. 
judgement have been promoted.

receive a judgement of the Andhra Pradesh High Cour t. We accept the 
judgement, and then say very well, the High Court h as pronounced a 
judgement, the vacancies must be filled according t o the number prior to 
restructuring. We have filled it accordingly. Now, the hon. Member asks me 
to make a judgement whether the 2002 decision was a n abuse of discretion or 
was it an arbitrary decision. How can I make such a  judgement? The 
Government of the day took a decision; the matter w as challenged in the 
Andhra Pradesh High Court. The Andhra Pradesh High Court has given a 
judgement. Our Government has accepted the judgemen t, and we have 
promoted, and we have filled all the vacancies acco rding to the unrestructured 
cadre. Every single vacancy has been filled in Patn a. I do not want to be 
judgemental about what happened 3 years ago or 5 ye ars ago. I can only deal 
with matters as they come before me. What came

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
before me is the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh Hig h Court. We did not,

*462. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA:† 
          SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether RBI has reported that the Scheduled Banks b usiness in the 
country in 2006-07 upto March 2 grew by 22.5 per ce nt as compared with 
23.4 per cent growth last year; 
(b) if so, whether Government will explain why inflatio n continued at 
over 6.4 per cent in the month of March, 2007 despi te claims of RBI that 
liquidity is less; 
(c) whether it is a fact that RBI has either been unabl e or perhaps 
unwilling to bring down inflation to less than 2.5 per cent; and 
(d) if so, what steps Government will take to introduce  fiscal measures to 
counter the hon activity of RBI? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) 
A Statement is placed in Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) As per the data released by the Reserve Bank of Ind ia (RBI), Bank 
Credit during 2006-07 (upto March 2,2007) grew by 2 2.5 percent compared 
to 23.4 per cent during the corresponding period of previous year. 
(b) Demand-supply gap in some agricultural commodities like wheat, 
pulses and edible oils, hardening international pri ces of various commodities 
including metals and crude oil, rapid rise in credi t, buoyant inflows of FDI 
and Fll reflecting positive investor sentiments, an d the high growth 
momentum of the economy have been the major reasons for inflation. 
(c) and (d) As monetary policy comes under the purview of RBI, a number 
of monetary measures were announced with the objective of containing

the excess liquidity in the system. The fixed repo rate under Liquidity 
Adjustment Facility (LAF) was increased by 25 basis  points to 7.75 per cent

per cent effective April 28,2007. As the monetary s tance has been aimed at 
maintaining price stability and anchoring inflation ary expectations without 
hurting the growth momentum, RBI in its Annual Poli cy Statement for 2007-
08, has reiterated its resolve to contain inflation  close to 5.00 per cent during

milk powder from February 9,2007

• Ban on futures trading in tur and urad from January  24,2007 and in

points in August, 2006 and further by 10-12.5 perce ntage points in 
January, 2007. Maintaining tariff value for assessi ng import duty-
unchanged at July, 2006 level.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, as I have said on more th an one 
occasion, the current inflation is largely triggere d by following four factors. 
Firstly, hardening of commodity prices, particularl y metals and crude oil. 
Secondly, a demand-supply mismatch, which started w ith sugar; then, wheat. 
When sugar prices eased, now it is in pulses. Third ly, increase in money 
supply. Thanks to capital inflows into the country.  And fourthly, increase in 
demand. Thanks to increase in public expenditure an d increase in credit. 
These factors have impacted inflation. Of course, o ne can draw one's own 
conclusion, but the fact is that the average inflat ion for 2006-07 has reached 
5.4 per cent. Before the UPA Government came, in th ree of the six years of 
the previous Government, the average inflation was more than 5.4 per cent. 
That does not give us any comfort. All I am pointin g out is that it Is not 
correct to say that Inflation is on the rise. ...(Interruptions)... Just a moment, 
please. Facts are facts. In three out of six years,  it was above 5.4 per cent and 
in three out of six years, it was less than 5.4 per  cent. ...(Interruptions)... It is, 
therefore, not correct to say that inflation is a p henomenon only under the 
UPA Government. The present inflation deserves 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
to be moderated; steps are being taken to moderate the present inflation. But 
it will be moderated in the long run only if the su pply-demand mismatch is 
met. I have pointed out how wheat production, paddy  production and pulses 
production have stagnated ever the last ten years. In fact, if you look at the 
production curve as well as the productivity curve,  it is a flat curve for wheat, 
paddy and pulses. There are other pressures like ha rdening of metal prices, 
crude oil prices and demand side pressures. What we  have done is, on the 
fiscal side, we have cut customs duties and excise duties. On the monetary 
side, RBI has increased the CRR in six steps from 5  to 6.5 per cent. It has 
also increased the risk weight for various kinds of  lending. That has had a 
moderating influence. In the medium to long-term, t he durable solution is 
increased supply. As long as supply of essentia! ar ticles, especially food 
articles, does not match up to demand, there will b e pressure on prices, and 
that is what is triggering the current inflation. 
Now, I have been asked to compare India with China.  China's inflation is 
reported to be between two and two-and-a-half per c ent. Even in China, in 
recent weeks, inflation seems to have moved up to t hree per cent and they are 
taking steps like we are taking, both on the moneta ry side and on the demand 
management. Beyond that, I cannot compare India and  China because I have 
no other information except what is reported about China, and I am not even 
competent to comment on the quality of information which China puts out. 
But on reported data, China's inflation is, indeed, lower than our inflation.

reviewed from time to time and changes are made. Bu t, at the moment, there 
are sectoral caps in some sectors. 
SHRI SU. THIRUNAVUKKARASAR: Sir, I asked about Tami l Nadu 
and Madhya Pradesh. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the answer I gave to Andh ra Pradesh 
also applies to Tamil Nadu. As far as Tamil Nadu is  concerned, if you take 
the Chennai regional office of the RBI, the amount of FDI inflow is 
equivalent to Rs. 10,690 crores between January, 20 00 and January, 2007. 
Now, if 
22 

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
you want to take Madhya Pradesh, the regional offic e is in Bhopal, which 
covers both Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh; the FD l flow during this 
period in the Bhopal office is Rs. 238 crores. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, the hon. Minister has stated that our investment 
in infrastructure has not kept pace with, the growt h of our GDP. Therefore, 
these figures are less relevant as figures themselv es and more relevant as to 
what percentage of the GDP they constitute—the inve stment in infrastructure 
as a percentage in GDP. Sir, it has been widely reported that India investment 
in infrastructure as a percentage of GDP is far les s than other comparable 
countries such a&China. Would the Hon. Minister giv e us some information 
as to where we stand vis-a-vis China and what the projections are as a 
percentage of GDP for the coming years? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the Investment Commission  which was 
appointed by the Government has estimated that for sustaining a high growth 
rate, we would require an investment of approximate ly 28 per cent to 32 per 
cent of GDP. But, as hon. Members are aware, we hav e already achieved an 
investment level of nearly 33.8 per cent of the GDP  in 2005-06. Sir the 
investment required to sustain a growth rate of abo ut 8 per cent is. already 
taking place. Now, of course, this FDl constitutes a very small proportion. If 
you take trillion-dollar GDP, what we are projectin g is 320 billion over a 
period of five years. That represents a small propo rtion of our GDP. The 
point is that the FDl in sectors where we allow FDl , it brings in new 
technology, brings in additional investment, brings  in new products and 
brings us the opportunity to enter new markets and which is why we invite 
FDl. But in terms of investment as a proportion of GDP, our investment ratio 
has improved in the last three to four years. I bel ieve in 2006-07 also, going 
by figures available from various sources, the inve stment to GDP ratio will 
be close to 35 per cent. That level of investment i s good enough to sustain the 
current rate of growth. But if we want to increase the rate of growth, we need 
more investment and some part of that investment ha s to indeed come from 
foreign sources. 
Dependence on oil imports  
*464. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of PETROLE UM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India is the third largest oil consuming 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
country in Asia and imports 70 per cent of its crude to meet its energy needs; 
(b) if so, what steps the Ministry has so far taken to tap more domestic 
reservoirs to help offset its growing dependence on  imports alongwith details 
thereof; and 
(c) the budgetary allocations made during the year 2007 -08 in comparison 
to the year 2006-07 to meet India's energy needs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) to (c) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
Referred to in reply to parts (a) to (c) of Rajya Sabha Starred Question  
No. 464 to be answered on 08.05.2007 regarding dependence  
on oil imports  
(a) Yes, Sir. During the year 2005, India was the t hird largest oil 
consuming 
country in Asia, after China and Japan. To meet the  demand, the country 
depended on imported crude to the extent of 73% during 2006-07. 
(b) To tap more domestic reservoirs to help reduce its growing 
dependence on imports, the Government has taken following steps: 
(i) Carving out more and more areas for exploration  for offer under 
various rounds of NELP. Six rounds of bids have so far been 
invited under NELP, in which 162 exploration blocks  have been 
awarded and 37 discoveries have already been made. 
(ii) Quicker development of discovered reserves for  enabling 
commencement of production. 
(iii) Use of stimulation techniques for increasing production from 
existing fields. 
(iv) Application of Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)/lmp roved Oil 
Recovery (IOR) techniques for increasing recovery f actor from 
existing fields. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Lt d. (ONGC) has 
taken up 15 fields for this purpose at an estimated  investment of 
Rs. 13651 crore, which would also help in accelerat ing oil 
production from these fields. 
24 

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Arresting decline from ageing fields. 
(vi) Acquisition of exploration acreages and produc ing properties 
overseas to bring in equity oil. 
(vii) Substitution of oil through use of non-conven tional source of 
energy such as bio-diesel, ethanol, etc. 
(c) As far as the oil and natural gas sector is con cerned, the PSU oil 
companies are financing the energy projects through  internal resource 
generation. As against the estimated plan outlay of  Rs. 36,800 crore for the 
PSU oil companies during 2006-07, the estimated out lay for 2007-08 is Rs. 
38,900 crore. The Government provided a subsidy of Rs. 2,549 crore 
towards marketing of domestic LPG ad PDS kerosene d uring 2006-07 from 
the fiscal budget, besides providing oil bonds of R s. 24,121 crore to the PSU 
oil marketing companies to compensate for the under -recoveries in 
marketing sensitive petroleum products. During the year 2007-08, the 
allocation towards subsidy for marketing domestic LPG and PDS kerosene is 
Rs. 2,680 crore.

Ethno-Graphic Studies on tribals by Anthropological Survey of India 
471. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of C ULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any system or process by wh ich constant 
and regular monitoring of tribals' progress is done  through ethnographic 
studies under the aegis of the Anthropological Survey of India; 
(b) if so, the prevalent system in this regard; 
(c) what degree of credibility does the ethno-graphic s tudies done by ASI 
enjoy; 
(d) whether it is a fact that sufficient studies are no t done on social status 
of tribals; and 
(e) the steps proposed to be taken to conduct frequent monitoring of all 
aspects of life of tribals? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a)  to (e) 
The Anthropoligical Survey of Indie conducts regula r ethno-graphic studies 
which help to monitor the progress of tribals. The ethno-graphic studies 
remain the Central approach of scientific investiga tion in the Survey. During 
Eleventh Plan the Anthropological Survey of India p roposes to study the 
indigenous knowledge systems of tribes, Man and Env inronment issues 
under the programme 'People of India and Cultural Diversity'. 
34 

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
The research findings of the Anthropological Survey  of India have 
considerable credibility and recognition. The Scien tists of Anthropological 
Survey of India are associated with Planning Commis sion bodies, Inter-State 
Council Secretariat, Jarwa Tribe related developmen t concerns and Forest 
Departments in respective Bio-sphere Zones of India . The publications 
brought out by the Survey have been widely reviewed  and acknolwedged for 
their ethnographic worthiness. 
Sufficient studies are done by Anthropological Surv ey of India on the 
social status of tribes of India. Around 100 books and 250 research papers 
have been published by the Scientists of the Survey on the subject. 
In the Eleventh Plan, the Survey has proposed inter vention as a strategy, 
instead of simple documentation of culture of triba ls. In this respect the 
project on 'Man in Biosphere' is a pointer. While i mplementing the project, 
Survey has also initiated dialogue with conservator  of forests and community 
leaders, so as to exchange field data based on inte nsive enthnographic studies 
of core villages in the biospheres.

Monetary measures to check inflation  
*480. SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Will the Minister of F INANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Reserve Bank of India  has taken certain 
monetary measures to check the prevailing inflation in the country; 
(b) if so, the details of such measures taken after Budget this year; and 
(c) whether these measures have been effective in contr olling inflationary 
trend in the markets; if so, the details thereof? 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and 
(b) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has taken a num ber of measures to 
anchor inflationary exceptions. With the objective of draining out excess 
liquidity and improving the efficacy of interest ra te signals, RBI, on March 
30, 2007 announced a hike in the fixed repo rate un der Liquidity Adjustment 
Facility (LAF) by 25 basis points to 7.75 per cent effective March 31, 2007. 
The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was increased 25 basis  points on March 3, 
2007. The CRR was further increased by 50 basis poi nts in two stages of 25 
basis points each, effective from fortnights beginn ing April 14 and April 28 
2007 to reach 6.5 per cent. To mop up excess liquid ity, the ceiling for the 
outstanding under Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS)  for the year 2007-08 
was revised from Rs. 80,000 crore to Rs. 95,000 cro re on April 24,2007 and 
further to Rs. 1,10,000 crore effective April 27, 2007. 
(d) Factors affecting inflation emanate from demand and  supply sides. 
Monetary policy has a cumulative and lagged effect on aggregate demand. 
Inflation, measured by variations in the wholesale price index (WPI) on a 
year-on-year basis, increased from 4.1 per cent at end-march 2006 to an 
intra-year peak of 6.7 per cent in end-January 2007  and remained firm in the 
range of 6.0—6.6 per cent in the succeeding weeks b efore moderating to 5.7 
per cent on march 31, 2007. As on April 21, 2007 in flation rate was 5.8 per 
cent on a year-on-year basis.

†3566. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will trie Min ister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Reserve Bank of India  have revised the 
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) twice in March, 2007 to check the inflation; 
(b) the amount sucked from the market circulation as a result of the said 
revision; 
(c) what is its effect on share market and the loss to the share holders as a 
result of it; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that mostly small and med ium investors 
suffered heavy losses among these investors; and 
(e) whether it is also a fact that it is indication of overheating of economic 
development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) and (b) To contain inflati onary 
expectations and in the light of current liquidity conditions, Reserve Bank of 
India (RBI) decided to increase the Cash Reserve Ra tio (CRR) of banks by 
0.25% of their net demand and time liabilities (NDT L) effective from the 
fortnight beginning 3rd March, 2007 from 5.75% to 6 .00%. As a result of the 
above increase in CRR, an amount of around Rs. 7,00 0 crore of resources of 
banks was expected to be absorbed. RBI, further on 30th March, 2007, 
increased the CRR of Banks by 0.50% of their NDTL i n two stages effective 
from the fortnights beginning 14th April, 2007 and 28th April, 2007, from 
6.00% to 6.25% and from 6.25% to 6.50% respectively . As a result of these 
increases in CRR, an additional amount of around Rs . 15,500 crore of 
resources of banks was expected to be absorbed. 
(c) and (d) Increase in CRR has no direct proportio nate positive 
correlation with increase/decrease in share prices,  which are affected due to 
various factors including plan, strategy and perfor mance of the listed 
companies, perception of the investors, investment by 
individuals/institutions/Flls, etc. 
(e) No, Sir.

†3570. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: Will the Minister of  FINANCE 
be pleased to state:

due to increase in rate of interest; and

projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI 
PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) Yes Sir, Infrastructure-re lated projects 
like all other projects are affected due to increas e in rate of interest. In 
particular, the existing projects are affected due to cost overruns. 
(b) Though interest rate risk is a critical factor,  it is not the only factor 
affecting the completion of the projects. Not many infrastructure projects 
have been stalled only due to rise- in interest rat es. Furthermore, the 
concessionaires normally make prior arrangements to  reduce the adverse 
effect of a rise in interest rate. Nowadays, long t erm loans are being 
negotiated and the reset periods are coming down. A lso the cost estimates of 
several public sector infrastructure projects have been revised upward to 
enable their timely completion.

3591. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of FINANC E be pleased

(a) whether Government are seriously considering any pr oposal of

eventuality of losing their expected income by vari ous reasons, i.e. flood, 
drought etc. as this mechanism is successfully going on in the western world; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof and by when it will be implemented

PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Agricultu ral Insurance 
Company of India Ltd. (AICIL) introduced Rainfall I nsurance Scheme 
known as "Varsha Bima" during 2004 south-west monso on period. Varsha

Evasion of stamp duty  
3592. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of FINANC E be pleased 
to state; 
(a) whether Government are aware about the large scale evasion of stamp 
duty for the registration of the properties and pay ment of property tax 
because of high percentage; 
(b) if so, whether Government have evolved any mechanis m to check the 
evasion of above duty/taxes as large number of buye rs and sellers prefer to 
pay black money or unaccounted money to seal the de al rather than pay the 
high taxes; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (S HRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (c) Under the Constitu tion of India, 
Stamp Duties (but not including rates of stamp duty ) fall under Entry 44 of 
the Concurrent List. Regarding rates of stamp duty,  the Central Government 
has powers to fix the rates in respect of 10 instru ments listed in Entry 91 of 
the Union List, whereas States have the powers in r espect of the remaining 
instruments by virtue of Entry 63 of the State List . The fixing of rates of 
stamp duty on properties is in the domain of the St ates. The revenue from 
stamp duties leviable within any State is assigned to that State by virtue of 
provisions of Article 268 of the Constitution. Thus , the stamp duty is 
collected and appropriated entirely by the States c oncerned. The 
administration of stamp duty laws (Central as well as the State) is entirely 
with the States. Therefore, it is for the States to  take necessary measures to 
prevent tax evasion in respect of stamp duties. In fact, most of the States have 
taken legal and administrative measures to deal wit h the issue of under-
valuation of properties for evading payment of stam p duty. During recent 
years, there is also a trend of States lowering the  rates of stamp duty to more 
moderate levels. Since this a matter concerning the  States, it is for the States 
to take necessary steps in this regard.

explicitly budgeting money upfront for pension by m aking a matching 
contribution into each employee's pension account. The transition from a 
defined benefit (DB) to a defined contribution (DC)  pension system would 
involve transition costs, as Government has to meet  liabilities arising from 
both types of systems for some time. This will grad ually decline and savings 
will appear when the entire set of existing pensioners cease to draw DB

the NPS, pending the passage of the Pension Fund Re gulatory and 
Development Authority Bill, 2005. There would be no  compulsion on

3613. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister o f 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the total demand and supply scenario of Kerosene in Rajasthan; 
(b) what is the yardstick for allocation of quota of Ke rosene to a State, and 
whether it has been fully applied in Rajasthan; 
(c) whether Government propose to increase the quota of  Kerosene for 
Rajasthan; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) by when the quota of Kerosene is likely to be i ncreased in the 
State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL): (a) to (e) Government 
of India allocates Kerosene to the States/Union Ter ritories (UTs) for 
distribution under the Public Distribution System ( PDS) on historical basis 
for the purpose of cooking and illumination only. I n accordance with the 
policy adopted by the Government of India in 2000, Kerosene (SKO) 
allocation for distribution under the Public Distri bution System (PDS) was 
reduced every year beginning 2001-02 till 2003-04, taking into account the 
number of LPG connections released in each State/Un ion Territory! While 
the initial allotment for 2004-05 was based on the criteria adopted hitherto, 
additional allocoations were made during the year t o meet urgent enlergent 
demand. For the years 2005-06 and 2006-07, allocati ons have been 
maintained at the level of 2004-05, including addit ional allocations made 
during that year. Allocations for first quarter for  2007-08 have been 
maintained at the level of 2006-07. 
In view of requests received from various State Gov ernments including 
Rajasthan for increasing the SKO allocation, the Go vernment of India 
commissioned the detailed study of Kerosene demand in the country, through 
the National Council of Applied Economic Research ( NCAER) in December, 
2004. NCAER submitted its report in October, 2005. NCAER has inter alia 
recommended to restrict the subsidy on Kerosene to BPL families only. 
Further, in order to formulate a long-term pricing policy, the Government 
had constituted an Inter-Ministerial Committee under the Chairmanship of 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
Dr. C. Rangarajan, Chairman, Economic Advisory Coun cil to the Prime 
Minister to examine different aspects of pricing an d taxation of petroleum 
products with a view to stabilizing/rationalizing t heir prices. The Committee 
submitted its report on 17.2.2006. The Committee ha s also inter alia 
recommended to restrict the subsidy on kerosene to BPL families only. The 
Government has accepted the recommendations of Dr. Rangarajan 
Committee Report and has decided 'in principle' tha t subsidy on PDS 
kerosene be limited to BPL families only. The propo sal to work out the 
modalities to implement this decision and for ratio nalizing the allocation of 
PDS kerosene among States/UTs is under the consider ation of the 
Government.

Artificial Recharge to Ground Water' identifying 4. 5 lakh sq. km. 
area in the country needing artificial recharge of ground water. 
The Master Plan has been circulated to all the Stat es/UTs for 
appropriate action. 
(ii) The CGWB has circulated Manual/Guide on techni ques of 
Artificial Recharge to Ground Water to the States/ Union 
Territories to enable them to formulate area specif ic artificial 
recharge schemes to check the declining trend of gr ound water 
levels. 
(iii) CGWB promotes rain water harvesting by conduc ting mass 
awareness/training programmes regularly in various parts of the 
country associating representatives of State Govern ment 
Organizations, Educational institutions, NGOs etc.

(iv) CGWB provides technical guidance on rain water  harvesting to 
various agencies including State Government agencie s, 
Educational Institutions, Resident Welfare Associat ions, Group 
Housing Societies, private entrepreneurs and individuals. 
(v) The CGWB has implemented 165 demonstrative rech arge projects 
in various State under the central sector scheme on  'Study of 
recharge to ground water' during the Ninth Plan. Th ese 
demonstrative projects have helped in evolving desi gns of suitable 
recharge structures in various hydrogeclogical envi ronments which 
can be replicated by the States. 
(vi) Implementation of demonstrative projects on ar tificial recharge and 
rain water harvesting by CGWB during 2006-07 in eig ht Over-
exploited/Criiical blocks and watersheds, worst aff ected by ground 
water depletion in 4 States namely Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. 
(c) 'Water' being a State subject, it is the respon sibility of the State 
Governments to formulate suitable regulations to co ntrol the development 
and management of ground water. However, to facilit ate enactment of 
suitable ground water legislation by the States, Mi nistry of Water Resources 
have criculated a draft Model Bill to regulate and control the development 
and management of ground water to ail the States an d Union Territories. The 
Bill was initially circulated in 1970 which has bee n recirculated in 1992, 
1996 and revised Model Bill in 2005 for adoption. 8  States/UTs viz. Andhra 
Pradesh, Goa, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu.  West Bengai, 
Lakshadweep and Pondicherry have enacted the legisl ation. 20 other 
States/UTs have also initiated the action for enact ing the legislation. The 
Model Bill provides for establishment of a Ground W ater Authority by the 
States/UT by way of notification in the Official Ga zette and appointment of 
technical personnel and other staff. This Authority  will issue notification of 
areas to regulate and control development and manag ement-of ground water, 
grant of permit to extract and use ground water in the notified area, 
registration of existing users in notified areas as  well as in non-notified areas 
and registration of drilling agencies. 
The Bill empowers the Authority to:— 
• Alter/amend or vary the terms of or cancel the perm it/certificate of 
registration. 
• Inspect and take copies of the relevant record or documents.

• Enter any property to inspect the well that has b een or is being 
stink, to take specimens of soil or other materials  or of water 
abstracted from such wells or order in writing the persons sinking a 
well to keep and preserve the samples of soils or water. 
• Direct the user of ground water to install water me asuring device on 
ground water abstraction structure. 
• Seize any equipment or device utilized far illegal sinking and demolish 
the work executed fully or partly. 
• Close down the abstraction of ground water or disco nnect its parts 
supply and demolish any hydrology work found to be illegal. 
• Enter and search any place where the offence under the Act has been 
or is being committed and order in writing the pers on who has been or 
is committing the offence not to abstract ground wa ter for a specified 
period. 
• Revised Model Bill, 2005 contains a new chapter on 'Rain Water 
Harvesting for Ground Water Recharge' and provides for imposition of 
stipulated conditions by the Municipal Corporations  or other local 
authorities for providing roof top rain water harve sting structures in 
building plan in an area of 100 sq.m or more, while  according approval 
for construction. 
• Identification of recharge worthy areas, issuance o f necessary 
guidelines for adoption of rain water harvesting fo r ground water 
recharge in these areas and issuance of direction b y the Authority to 
the concerned Department to include rainwater harve sting in all 
development schemes falling under notified areas. 
• Promotion of rainwater harvesting and artificial re charge by the 
Authority through Mass Awareness and Training Programmes. 
In addition, the Bill empowers the State/UT Governm ents to make rules 
to remove the difficulties, if any, in giving effec t to the provisions of the Act 
within two years of the date of commencement of the  Act. It has a provision 
for imposing penalties for offences committed again st the provisions of the 
Act. The Bill also provides for appeals by the aggr ieved persons to Appellate 
Authority as specified by the State/UT Government.   -

WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) The  
National Water Policy, 2002 (NWP) has been adopted by the National Water 
Resources Council in April, 2002. 
(b)The salient features of the National Water Polic y, 2002 are given in the 
Statement (See below). 
(c) The NWP states that its success will depend ent irely on envolving and 
maintaining a national consensus and commitment to its underlying 
principles and objectives. For achieving the desire d objectives, the NWP 
stipulates formulation of State Water Policy backed  with an operational 
action plan in a time bound manner. State Water Pol icy has been adopted by 
the States of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Himachal  Pradesh, Orissa, Goa, 
Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and UTs of Daman and Diu a nd Dadra and Nagar 
Haveli. The Ministry of Water Resources has request ed all other States for 
early formulation and adoption of the State Water P olicy in the 12th Meeting 
of National Water Board held on 5.1.2007. 
Statement  
Salient features of National Water Policy, 2002 
• Water is a precious national resource and its planning, development and 
management should be governed by national perspectives. 
238 

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
• A well developed information system for water relat ed data at national/ 
State level should be established with a network of  data banks and data 
bases integrating and strengthening the existing Ce ntral and State-level 
agencies. 
• Water resources development and management will hav e to be planned 
for a hydrological unit. Appropriate river basin or ganisations should be 
established for the planned development and managem ent of the river 
basins. 
• Water should be made available to water short areas  by transfer from 
other areas including transfer from one river basin  to another, after 
taking into account the requirements of the areas/basins. 
• Planning of water resources development projects sh ould, as far as 
possible, be for multi-purpose with an integrated a nd multi-disciplinary 
approach having regard to human and ecological aspe cts including 
those of disadvantaged sections of the society. 
• In the allocation of water, first priority should b e given for drinking 
water, followed by irrigation, hydro-power, ecology , agro-industries 
and non-agricultural industries, navigation and other uses, in that order. 
• The exploitation of ground water should be regulate d with reference to 
recharge possibilities and consideration of social equity. The 
detrimental environmental consequences of over-expl oitation of ground 
water need to be effectively prevented 
• Careful planning is necessary to ensure that constr uction and 
rehabilitation activities proceed simultaneously. A  skeletal national 
policy on resettlement and rehabilitation needs to be formulated such 
that project affected persons share the benefits th rough proper 
rehabilitation. 
• Adequate emphasis needs to be given to the physical  and financial 
sustainability of existing water resources faciliti es. There is need to 
ensure that the water charges for various users sho uld be fixed such as 
to cover at least the operation and maintenance cha rges initially and a 
part of the capital costs subsequently. 
• Management of the water resources for diverse uses should 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
incorporate a participatory approach by involving u sers and other 
stakeholders alongwith various governmental agencie s, in an effective 
and decisive manner. 
• Private sector participation should be encouraged i n planning, 
development and management of water resources proje cts for diverse 
uses, wherever feasible. 
• Both surface water and ground water should be regul arly monitored for 
quality. Effluents should be treated to acceptable levels and standards 
before discharging them into natural streams, Minim um flow should be 
ensured in the perennial streams for maintaining ecology. 
• Efficieny of utilization should be improved in all the diverse uses of 
water and conservation consciousness promoted throu gh education, 
regulation, incentives and disincentives. 
• There should be a Master Plan for flood control and  management for 
each flood prone basin. In flood control and manage ment, the strategy 
should be to reduce the intensity of floods. 
• Land erosion by sea or river should be minimized by  suitable cost-
effective measures. Indiscriminate occupation of, a nd economic 
activity in coastal areas and flood plain zones should be regulated. 
• Needs of drought-prone areas should be given priori ty in the planning 
of project for development of water resources. Thes e areas should be 
made less vulnerable through various measures. 
• The water sharing/distribution amongst the States s hould be guided by 
a national perspective with due regard to water res ources availability 
and needs within the river basin. 
• Training and research efforts should be intensified  as an integral part of 
water resources development.

meeting at Srinagar Airport on 22nd April, 2007. Th e Government of India's 
total silence on this important issue of national s ecurity and the status of the 
State of Jammu and Kashmir, it has a direct nexus a lso with Indo-Pak 
relations. It also adversely affected the question of employment of Armed 
Forces in combating insurgency and terrorism in the  country, the 
Government's policy in this regard and approach also." 
Sir, I wish to submit that a meeting took place on the 22nd of April. Syed 
Ali Shah Geelani was under treatment in a hospital and he, thereafter, 
travelled to Srinagar. The fact that he was travell ing to Srinagar was not a 
secret to the Government of India, and it was not a  secret to the State 
Government either. The preparations that were being made at the Srinagar 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2007] 
Airport, building of platform-, microphones, receiv ing him, were not being done 
in secret or surreptitiously. They were well within  the knowledge of the State 
Government and if the Union Government did not know  of it, or claims that it 
did not know of it, then, that is an additional poi nt of concern . that I wish to 
raise. 
Thereafter, Syed Ali Shah Geelani lands at Srinagar  Airport and he was 
escorted to this pre-arranged built dais upon which  he addresses the 
assembly. I do not know how much the assembly was, in which, it is reported 
— this was widely broadcast and reported — that slo gans were raised, anti-
India slogans were raised, and there were also flag s demonstrating support to 
the Lashkar-e-Taiba. You know very well, Sir, and the House also knows t ha 
the Lashkar-e-Taiba is an organisation that admittedly, just a few mont hs 
back, a few weeks back, perhaps, had committed a gr ave act of terrorism 
where two hundred plus citizens of India lost their  lives on a Bombay train. It 
is also well enough known, Sir, that the day Syed A li Shah Geelani was 
making the statement and was receiving applause fro m those that were 
claiming to be the adherents of the Lashkar-e-Taiba, that very day, threats 
were received and two LeT terrorists were arrested here, in Delhi. Now, if the 
Government of India thereafter, two or. three days later, orders that Sayed Ali 
Shah Geelani was to be kept under house-arrest and some one or two people 
were also taken into custody, that reaily begs the question; and the question 
is, if they knew that he was coming, why was, in th e first instance, a meeting 
permitted at SrinagarAirport?And, if that meeting w as permitted, knowing that 
he was going to address it, it stands to reason, Si r, that the Central 
Government has something to explain, to account for , and we.have a right to 
know from the Central Government in this regard. 
Sir, the second issue, there are four issues that I  have listed here, is 
regarding the status of Jarnmu and Kashmir. The hon . Prime Minister, on a 
recent visit, in his speech, spoke of the new State  of Jarnmu, Kashmir and 
Ladakh. It could be a new way of referring to the S tate. But, it is an unusual 
way and if it reflects a change in the thinking of the Central Government, then, 
we have a right to know. The hon. Prime Minister ha s also spoken, time and 
again, of soft borders, making borders irrelevant, etc., that he desires, by his 
own admission, to have breakfast in Amritsar, lunch  in Lahore and dinner in 
Kabul. These are very worthwhile aspirations. I don 't see them even on the 
horizon. And, India is the victim of continued acts of terrorism, 
270 

[8 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
promotion of terrorism by Pakistan. And, if this is  stated by all intelligence 
agencies, I am surprised, Sir, by the statements of  the hon. Prime Minister. 
We know that thereafter and we are told that there are a number of 
committees that the Prime Minister has instituted, which are now going to look 
into the status of Jarnmu and Kashmir. I remind, Si r, the House—and, no 
doubt, the Prime Minister has many advisers—that on  the 22nd of February, 
1994, then! had the honour of being a Member of the  other House— a 
unanimous Resolution was passed, unanimous, which w as then read out by 
the then Speaker of the Lok Sabha and approved also , by acclaim, by late 
Shri Narsimha Rao, who was then the Prime Minister.  Just one or two lines 
from that, Sir, merit some mention here or even if I don't quote them exactly, 
they certainly mention merit inasmuch as the House had then resolved that 
the State of Jarnmu and Kashmir is an integral part  of India. And, it had firmly 
declared, in addition that the State is an integral  part of India, any attempt to 
separate it from the rest of the country will be re sisted by all necessary 
means; two, that India has a willing capacity to fi rmly counter all designs 
againsi its unity, sovereignty and territorial inte grity; and demands—and it was 
the House that then demanded—that Pakistan must vac ate the areas of the. 
Indian State of Jarnmu and Kashmir which they have occupied through 
aggression and resolves that ail attempts to interf ere in the internal affairs of 
India will be met resolutely" I am sure the hon. Pr ime Minister has number of 
advisors who Will inform him that the State of Jarn mu and Kashmir comprise 
the whole of Ladakh, it comprise what are commonly referred to as the 
northern territories; and it also comprise the enti re Pak occupied Kashmir, the 
area west of Kishanganga. When has, Sir, Parliament  addressed this 
resolution again and changed its mind about the sta tus or other aspects, or 
the integral aspect of the State of Jarnmu and Kash mir? We have seen many 
changes. The concern that I have, Sir, is that thes e changes are being made 
with insufficient information to Parliament. We rea lly do not know 'what is 
being done. On one occasion, the hon. Prime Ministe r advised us that he did 
not discuss such issues in public. I am astonished at that. The hon. Prime 
Minister is ready to discuss all aspects of Foreign  Policy with everyone else 
but the Opposition or with the Parliament. 
May I, Sir, also submit that the reason why India's  relations with Pakistan 
go wrong, which is the third aspect, is that increa singly I see a tendency on 
the part of this Government, which I find a.greatly  disturbing tendency, to 
outsource our Foreign Policy? Many years back when late Indira Gandhi was 
very ably leading the country, I had occasion to di scuss—I was then, too, a 
Member of Parliament—and suggest to her that it wou ld be a grave

error on our part to have India's Foreign Policy, i n regard to Sri Lanka, being 
determined in Tamil Nadu. Today, it is again being determined like that. 
Sir, I have written to the hon. Prime Minister that  India-Pakistan relations 
are not a synonym simply for the relationship betwe en the two Punjabs. It is 
not just a question of West and East Punjab having good relations what 
somebody commented the other day as a relationship of 'Jaffiyan.' Sir, 
'jaffiyan' means that they could embrace each other  whenever they wish to. 
But 'jaffiyan' is not any equivalent to a policy. I  wrote formally twice to the hon. 
Prime Minister, to which I did not receive a single  reply and I was astonished 
by that. My plea was: Do not let the then Chief Min ister of Punjab conduct an 
independent Foreign Policy. Sir, I submit that duri ng this year's new-year 
celebrations, he, in fact, went to the extent of br inging a plane-load of his own 
guests from Pakistan without visa, without permissi on, to Rajasthan. They 
went to a place called Khimsar to spend time, the w hole of the new-year 
celebration, only because the owner of that little fortress, Khimsar, and he 
were together at school in Dehradoon or some such thing. 
Sir, I also wish to submit that if you make your Fo reign Policy, for example 
in the East, subject to what the Government of Assa m says in regard to 
ULFA, or subject to the Government of Manipur, this  is very dangerous. This 
kind of fragmentation of the country's Foreign Poli cy and leaving it to the 
charge of the State Governments is possibly the wor st thing that can be done 
from the point of view of Indian Foreign Policy and  India's Security which is 
what brings me to the fourth aspect—the employment of armed forces. Sir, 
the employment of Armed Forces is a function and a responsibility which is 
directly of the Central Government, the Union Gover nment, and no one else. I 
have witnessed examples earlier, Sir, when the depl oyment of Army in 
Manipur was played with because it was advantageous  to the ruling party, for 
the Government of Manipur, to do so. Sir, I don't w ant to go into that aspect 
here, but, I have seen how the Army is now made sub servient to the interests 
of the ruling establishment. Sir, you cannot have a  decision of Army, its 
deployment....

to employ it, when to employ it and what force to e mploy it, is entirely of the
